# Token interference and forgetting

**Trajectory: LMEnt-1B-6E, 15-shot `drop-same-prop`, top-10% by co-occurrence.**
Run 2026-08-08; **respecified 2026-09-12** — exposure is now split into its gold and
rival components and the interval-restricted exposure term is gone (see *The models*).
**Every number in this doc is regenerated by
`analysis/strain_diagnostics.py`** — run it and diff the log rather than trusting the
prose. Saved raw outputs:

| file | holds |
|---|---|
| `data/artifacts/features/strain_diagnostics_specE.txt` | all twelve diagnostic sections, as printed — section 12 covers the tokenization claims (which tokens the DF cutoff removes, and canonical forms vs aliases) that were previously stated only in the `strain.py` docstring |
| `data/artifacts/features/strain_diagnostics_specE.json` | the same, machine-readable — including all 150 draws of the reported permutation test (`permutation_reported`) |

The rendered HTML report is **not** kept in the repo — it is several MB of inlined
plotly and every number on it now comes from the JSON above. Regenerate it on demand
with `analysis/report_token_strain.py` (see *Reproducing*); its only inputs are the
diagnostics JSON and the panel.

The pre-respecification permutation draws (`null_control_15shot_top10_namelen.json`)
are kept as the record of the pooled-exposure run; its summary numbers are quoted
inline above.

## Conclusion

**Subject-side token interference predicts forgetting in the hypothesised direction,
but the evidence stops short of establishing it as a token-identity effect.**

Four findings, in descending order of confidence:

1. **Subject strain is a significant predictor, and the largest of the token-level
   effects** — more entities sharing the subject's tokens, more forgetting. +0.188
   log-odds per log-unit (p=0.0021), which is **+0.291 per standard deviation, an
   odds ratio of 1.34**; it adds chi2(2)=18.3 (p=1.1e-04) over a baseline that
   already holds gold and rival exposure, popularity, name length, and relation and
   window fixed effects. One control is larger per SD — rival-answer exposure at
   −0.385 — so this is the biggest *token-level* effect, not the biggest overall.
2. **Name length is not the confound on this subset** (chi2(2)=2.9, p=0.23). This
   matters because on a broader fact set it is: strain rises steeply with how many
   tokens a name has, and there name length dominates. Restricting to the
   high-co-occurrence decile removes that.
3. **But a permutation test does not clear significance** (p=0.079). Rebuilding the
   token index with tokens randomly reassigned across entities — preserving each
   entity's token *count* and the corpus-wide token frequencies, destroying only
   which token belongs to whom — leaves 11 of 150 scrambled indices scoring at
   least as high as the real one. So we cannot rule out that the effect comes from
   structural properties the shuffle preserves rather than from actual token
   collisions. The p-value is **insensitive to the exposure specification**: 0.073
   under the old pooled control, 0.073 pooled-static-only, 0.079 here.
4. **Token-sharing rivals and answer-competing rivals point in opposite
   directions** — strain harmful (+0.188, p=0.002), rival-answer co-occurrence
   protective (−0.173, p=0.034). The *directions* are robust: strain is positive in
   all four exposure specifications tried and distract negative in all six nesting
   steps. That is enough to rule out strain being rival exposure remeasured, which
   is the load-bearing use of this contrast.
   **The magnitudes are not independently identified**, though — the two mutually
   suppress (see *Mutual suppression* below), and distract is **not** significant in
   strain's absence (p=0.18 at the baseline's controls). Do not quote its p=0.034 as
   a standalone result.
   And the protective term is most likely prominence, not competition: what removes
   its significance is adding `s_pop`/`o_pop` (p=0.021 → 0.212), i.e. Wikipedia
   page popularity, which measures real-world notability independently of the corpus.
   A subject seen beside many candidate answers is mostly just a well-covered
   subject.

The object side shows nothing (−0.027, p=0.69), and the effect is concentrated in
two of five relations rather than broad-based.

**Read this as: the hypothesis survived its sharpest test but did not pass it.**

---

## What was done

**Outcome.** 15-shot `drop-same-prop` recall sweep over 13 checkpoints
(50,000 → 658,032; no step 0). Demonstrations never share the query's relation, so
in-context answer-type leakage is designed out. 1,452 facts raw → **1,310** after
dropping 142 `excluded` (the answer or an alias occurs inside the question, so they
are answerable by copying the prompt). Accuracy 0.147 → 0.415.

**Fact subset.** `num_shared_chunks >= 42` — the **top 10.2%** of popqa-kas by
subject/answer co-occurrence.

This is a high-frequency slice, **not** a fixed-frequency one: across the 623 facts
actually modelled, `num_shared_chunks` runs min 42, median 606, p90 7,933, max
101,081. That matters for one specific reading of the results. `l_shared_static` —
which *is* `num_shared_chunks` — comes out null here (p=0.86), and the cheap
explanation would be "restricted range, there is no frequency variation left to
predict with". There is: ~13x spread from median to p90. So gold exposure being null
is a fact about this subset, not an artifact of having squeezed the variance out of
it, and note the *rival* exposure term is significant on the very same subset
(−0.173, p=0.034). What the restriction *does* buy is that the frequency confound is
much weaker than on the full fact set, which is why name length stops mattering here.

Keep this in view when comparing against a whole-dataset hazard curve: the protective
effect of exposure is strong across the full range and flat inside the top decile.

**Panel.** One row per (fact, checkpoint window) where the fact was **correct at the
window's start** — a discrete-time hazard design; a fact cannot be forgotten if it
was never known. 12 windows, **4,163 rows / 1,006 forgetting events / 713 facts**.
After dropping relations with <100 rows or <20 events: **3,932 / 878 / 623 facts
over 5 relations** (`capital` 2,401, `capital of` 721, `religion` 335, `sport` 250,
`country` 225).

**Features.** Competitors are counted as **entities** (Wikidata QIDs), not surface
strings, so two distinct entities written "Buffalo" count twice and an entity never
competes with its own aliases. Canonical surface forms only — Wikidata alias lists
are a knowledge-base artifact, not evidence a token appeared in training.

### Every column, in words

| column | meaning |
|---|---|
| `forgot` | **outcome.** 1 if the fact was correct at the window's start and wrong at its end. |
| `subj_strain`, `obj_strain` | **the hypothesis.** How many *other entities* share ≥1 token with this fact's subject / object. Computed as the **size of the union** of rival sets across the entity's tokens — not a sum, not a mean — excluding the fact's own other endpoint. |
| `subj_strain_w`, `obj_strain_w` | the same, restricted to entities that appeared in *this window*. |
| `shared_static` | **gold exposure.** Chunks where the subject co-occurs with the true answer. Exactly equal to `num_shared_chunks`. **In the baseline.** |
| `distract_static` | **rival exposure.** Chunks pairing the subject with a *different* valid answer for the same relation. **In the baseline.** |
| `shared_w`, `distract_w` | the same, restricted to this window. Carried in the panel; not in the model (see *The models*). |
| `evidence_static`, `evidence_w` | `shared + distract`, the old pooled exposure control. Retained in the panel for the robustness row; **no longer in the model.** |
| `s_pop`, `o_pop` | Wikipedia page popularity for subject / object, as defined by PopQA (Mallen et al., 2023). Real-world popularity, not exposure. Not sitelinks: `s_pop` reaches 15.1M. |
| `s_ntok`, `o_ntok` | **name length.** Number of tokens in the subject / object name, after the frequency cutoff drops `the`/`of`. |
| `s_own_rare`, `o_own_rare` | **F1, ownership.** This fact's evidence as a *share*: `num_shared_chunks ÷ \|all chunks carrying the entity's rarest token\|`. Low = the fact's signal is a small slice of everything bearing those tokens. |
| `s_rivals_rare`, `o_rivals_rare` | **F1, rivals.** How many other entities carry that rarest token. |
| `ratio_static`, `ratio_w` | **F2, alt-answer.** `(shared+1) ÷ (shared+distract+2)`, where `distract` counts chunks pairing the subject with a *different* valid answer for the same relation. High = the evidence the model saw was mostly the right answer. |

All continuous predictors enter as `log(1+x)` (prefix `l_`), so a unit is roughly an
e-fold change in the raw quantity.

### The models

Logistic regression on `forgot`, standard errors clustered by fact. Every model
contains `C(prop)` and `C(window)` — a separate intercept per relation and per
window — so comparisons are *within* relation and *within* window.

```
BASE      = forgot ~ l_shared_static + l_distract_static + l_s_pop + l_o_pop
                     + C(prop) + C(window)
NAMELEN   =        + l_s_ntok + l_o_ntok
STRAIN    =        + l_subj_strain + l_obj_strain          (or the _w variants)
F1        =        + l_s_own_rare + l_o_own_rare + l_s_rivals_rare + l_o_rivals_rare
F2        =        + ratio_static                          (or ratio_w)
```

**Exposure is split, and static only.** Two deliberate choices.

*Split*, because `shared` and `distract` correlate at only spearman 0.74 and act in
opposite directions — pooling them into `evidence` hid a real distinction and cost
nothing to undo (every `shared_*`/`distract_*` column was already in the panel).

*Static only*, because a 50,000-step window samples a constant ~46% of **every**
fact's chunks (50,000/109,672 = 0.456; measured 0.453 ± 0.039 per row, and the longer
final window sits at 0.529 = 58,032/109,672 — which independently confirms the
`WindowMap` epoch arithmetic). The fraction is the same for every fact, so in log
space the windowed count is the static one minus a constant —
`l_evidence_w = 0.997·l_evidence_static − 0.771`, R²=0.998, residual sd 0.084 against
an outcome sd of 1.867 — and `C(window)` already absorbs that offset. Carrying both
left the exposure coefficients unidentified (SEs ~4x the coefficients, p=0.59/0.79)
while adding nothing: dropping the windowed term moved the strain LR chi2 by **0.0**
and the coefficient from +0.1894 to +0.1895.

This is a **sampling-uniformity** argument and is *not* the reason windowed **strain**
is degenerate — that one is genuine saturation (~90% of entities active every window).
Do not merge the two explanations.

So the table row **`+ strain | name length`** is literally
`BASE + NAMELEN + STRAIN` — the pipe reads "strain, *given* name length is already
controlled". Nothing is dropped; terms are only ever added.

**Why the same model shows two different χ² values.** A likelihood-ratio test needs a
reference model, and the doc uses two:

| reference | asks |
|---|---|
| `BASE` (exposure only) | does this add anything over frequency and popularity? |
| `BASE + NAMELEN` | does this add anything *beyond name length* — the confound that explains the same association on broader fact sets? |

`BASE + NAMELEN + STRAIN` scores **χ²(4)=21.2** against `BASE` (4 added terms: 2 name
length + 2 strain) and **χ²(2)=18.3** against `BASE + NAMELEN` (2 added terms: strain
only). Same fitted model, different question. **The second is the one that matters**,
because strain and name length are correlated, so a comparison that credits strain
with name length's work is not evidence about interference.

Name length enters as post-cutoff token count only. `charlen` (raw string length)
measures the same construct — spearman 0.879 subj / 0.840 obj on the **broad** panel,
0.833 / 0.792 on this one — and splitting collinear credit between them makes both
uninterpretable; it is kept in the panel as a robustness check. (The often-quoted
"0.88" is the broad-panel figure; see diagnostics section 11.)

---

## Results

### Model comparison

```
model (all include C(prop) + C(window))   pseudoR2   vs BASE          vs BASE+NAMELEN
BASE  exposure + popularity                 0.1554   --               --
BASE + NAMELEN                              0.1561   chi2(2)=  2.9    --
                                                     p=0.23
BASE + STRAIN                               0.1577   chi2(2)=  9.4    (not nested)
                                                     p=9.0e-03
BASE + NAMELEN + STRAIN                     0.1605   chi2(4)= 21.2    chi2(2)= 18.3
                                                     p=2.9e-04        p=1.1e-04   <-- headline
BASE + NAMELEN + F1                         0.1637   chi2(6)= 34.7    chi2(4)= 31.7
                                                     p=5.0e-06        p=2.2e-06
BASE + NAMELEN + F2                         0.1562   chi2(3)=  3.3    chi2(1)=  0.4
                                                     p=0.34           p=0.53
```

Read the **right-hand column** for anything about interference; the middle column
credits each feature with name length's contribution as well.

The F1 row is optimizer-sensitive: its four correlated terms leave the likelihood
nearly flat, and BFGS has landed on several nearby values in different sessions.
Reproducible within a session, so do not quote it to three significant figures. The
strain rows are stable.

**F1 now tests something different.** Its numerator, `num_shared_chunks`, is
`shared_static` — a baseline term since the respecification — so `own_rare` is
`l_shared_static` minus the log pool size, and the family effectively isolates the
**pool denominator**. That is arguably a cleaner test than before, but it is not the
test the column table describes. F1 rose from chi2(4)=28.1 to 31.7 accordingly.

**F2 is now near-vacuous by construction.** `ratio = (shared+1)/(shared+distract+2)`
is a function of two baseline terms, so its increment (chi2(1)=0.4, p=0.53) mostly
asks whether one particular nonlinear combination of them adds anything. It was
already null before, so no finding is lost — but the number should not be read as an
independent test of the alt-answer hypothesis.

### Coefficients (static strain, name length controlled, clustered by fact)

Predictors are `log(1+x)` but **not standardised**, so raw coefficients are per
log-unit of their own variable and are **not comparable across rows**. The
`coef x SD` column rescales each to "change in log-odds per 1 SD of that predictor",
which is the column to read when ranking effects. Sorted by that.

```
                    coef   Std.Err.   SD(x)   coef x SD   OR per SD    P>|z|
l_distract_static -0.1734   0.0816    2.223    -0.385       0.68      0.0335
l_subj_strain     +0.1883   0.0612    1.547    +0.291       1.34      0.0021  <- hypothesis
l_o_pop           -0.2189   0.0781    1.327    -0.290       0.75      0.0051
l_s_ntok          -0.8034   0.3443    0.291    -0.234       0.79      0.0196
l_s_pop           -0.1132   0.0842    1.459    -0.165       0.85      0.1785
l_o_ntok          +0.4867   0.3930    0.249    +0.121       1.13      0.2156
l_obj_strain      -0.0272   0.0682    1.498    -0.041       0.96      0.6895
l_shared_static   -0.0131   0.0750    1.680    -0.022       0.98      0.8616
```

Two things this reordering changes:

**Subject strain is the largest of the token-level effects**, not a small one. On raw
coefficients name length looks ~4x bigger (−0.80 vs +0.19); that is an artifact of
spread. `s_ntok` is 1–6 tokens with median 1, so its log SD is 0.29, while
`subj_strain` runs 0–422 with log SD 1.55. Per SD the ordering reverses: +0.291 for
strain against −0.234 for subject name length. A standard-deviation move in subject
strain multiplies the odds of forgetting by **1.34**. Only `l_distract_static` is
larger per SD (−0.385), so strain is the second-largest effect in the model overall.

**Exposure splits into a null and a real effect.** Gold co-occurrence
(`l_shared_static`, identical to `num_shared_chunks`) is a *tightly estimated* zero:
−0.013, se 0.075, p=0.86. Rival co-occurrence is protective: −0.173, se 0.082,
p=0.034 — more chunks pairing the subject with some *other* valid answer, less
forgetting. Note the sign: it is **opposite** to strain, which is the cleanest
available evidence that strain is not rival-answer exposure measured a second way.

**Mutual suppression.** These two estimates are entangled, and the nesting shows how:

```
model                               l_distract_static      l_subj_strain
1 distract alone + FE               -0.2503 (p<0.001)          --
2 + gold exposure                   -0.1299 (p=0.021)          --
3 + popularity  (= BASE)            -0.0988 (p=0.212)          --
4 + name length (= BASE+NAMELEN)    -0.1092 (p=0.179)          --
5 + strain      (= reported)        -0.1734 (p=0.034)   +0.1883 (p=0.002)
6 as 5, gold exposure dropped       -0.1816 (p=0.011)   +0.1899 (p=0.002)
```

The sign never reverses, but the significance is not stable. Each predictor roughly
doubles the other's increment — distract goes chi2(1)=3.9 → 9.1 when strain is added,
strain goes chi2(2)=13.1 → 18.3 when distract is added, and strain's coefficient goes
+0.153 → +0.188 — which is what two negatively correlated (−0.154) predictors with
opposite-signed effects do to each other. So read *directions* as robust and
*magnitudes* as jointly determined.

**The protective term is most likely prominence, not competition.** Row 3 is the
diagnostic: what removes distract's significance is adding `s_pop`/`o_pop`, Wikipedia
page popularity, which measures real-world notability independently of the corpus — not
name length (row 4 changes almost nothing). A subject appearing beside many candidate
answers is, to a large extent, simply a subject Wikipedia covers well. Treat it as a
control that intermittently reaches significance, not a finding about competition.

Every standard error in the table is now under 0.40, against 0.83 before. Two rows
still have |coef/se| < 1 (`l_shared_static`, `l_obj_strain`) but for the opposite
reason to before: they are precise nulls, not unidentified coefficients.

Raw forgetting rate by subject-strain quartile — no model, no controls:

```
Q1 low   0.207      Q3       0.229
Q2       0.175      Q4 high  0.283
```

### Permutation test (150 draws, name length in the baseline)

```
real token index      chi2 = 18.3
null distribution     min 0.0 | median 6.2 | max 41.8 | mean 7.7 (sd 7.6)
permutations >= real  11 of 150
empirical p           0.079
```

**Insensitive to the exposure control.** 150 draws under each of three baselines:

```
pooled static+windowed (old)   obs 19.26   10/150   p=0.073
pooled static only             obs 19.27   10/150   p=0.073
gold+rival static (current)    obs 18.28   11/150   p=0.079
```

relation      rows  events   l_subj_strain
all (5)       3932     878   +0.188 (se 0.061, p=0.002)
capital       2401     410   +0.040 (se 0.095, p=0.676)
capital of     721     123   +0.713 (se 0.217, p=0.001)
religion       335     102   +0.469 (se 0.141, p=0.001)

```

static on top of windowed   chi2(2)= 2.6   p=0.27
```

## How the results support the conclusion

**For the hypothesis.** The subject-strain coefficient is positive and significant
in exactly the predicted direction, it survives an exposure baseline built
specifically so that frequency cannot explain it, the raw quartiles rise without any
model, and name length — the confound that explains the same association on broader
fact sets — is not significant here (chi2(2)=2.9, p=0.23). It also points the
opposite way to rival-answer exposure, so it is not that control under another name.

**Against treating it as established.** The permutation test is the one that
distinguishes "which tokens collide" from "some structural property correlated with
having many tokens". At p=0.079 it does not separate them, and that figure barely
moves across exposure specifications (0.073–0.079), so it is not an artifact of how
exposure is controlled. And the pooled effect is carried by `capital of` (+0.71) and
`religion` (+0.47) while being null in `capital` (+0.04), which is 61% of the rows,
and in `sport` and `country`. A mechanism that operated on token collision should not
be that relation-specific.

**On the object side**, nothing: −0.027, p=0.69. If the mechanism were competition at
the decoding step — many entities competing for the answer's tokens — the object side
is where it should appear most strongly. It does not.

**The windowed form is uninformative here**, as on every panel tried: about 90% of
the 19,384-entity universe is active in every 50,000-step window, so "which
competitors appeared since the last checkpoint" is effectively "all of them".
Windowed strain is a near-copy of static strain, and adds nothing to it.

---

## What would settle it

1. **Finer checkpoints — and the requirement is far stricter than once estimated.**
   An entity occupying `k` of the ~10.5M chunks is only commonly *absent* from a
   window covering fraction `f` when `f <~ 1/k`, and `f = steps / 109,672`. The
   relevant `k` is denominator-sensitive, so all of them (diagnostics section 11):

   ```
   median over per-fact object rows (14,267)   k =   305  ->  windows <~  360 steps
   median over unique object entities (7,462)  k =   101  ->  windows <~ 1,086 steps
   median over objects IN THIS PANEL (495)     k = 3,679  ->  windows <~    30 steps
   ```

   The last line is the one that governs, because the panel is the **top decile by
   co-occurrence** — its objects are an order of magnitude more frequent than the
   corpus median, which is the whole point of the subset. So windows would need to
   be ~30 steps, not the "1–2K steps, 25–50x finer" this doc previously claimed
   (that figure came from the per-fact 305 and was optimistic even for it).

   At ~110 checkpoints per epoch the 6-epoch release offers ~1,000-step spacing,
   still **~30x too coarse** for the facts analysed here. So the *temporal* form of
   the hypothesis is not merely under-resourced at 13 checkpoints — it is out of
   reach at any granularity LMEnt ships, and testing it would need either a custom
   checkpoint schedule or a lower-frequency fact subset (which reintroduces the
   name-length confound the top-decile restriction was chosen to remove). That
   tension is the real obstacle, and it is worth stating plainly rather than as an
   evaluation-count estimate.
2. **A corpus-wide competitor universe.** Competitors are currently the 19,384
   entities in popqa-kas, against millions in the corpus, so strain is attenuated —
   and attenuated more for rare entities. The mention annotations are 32 GB of
   streamable `.csv.gz` (`dataset-tokenized/part-*.csv.gz`), not the 127 GB
   Elasticsearch tarball.
3. **More relations at this exposure level.** Five relations, two carrying the
   effect, is too thin to tell a mechanism from a relation-specific quirk.

---

## Caveats

1. **713 facts / 878 events.** Small. Null results here are weak evidence; the
   positive one needs replication before it is built on.
2. **Relation mix is extreme** — `capital` and `capital of` are 79% of rows, and
   `occupation` and `place of birth` drop out entirely. Relation fixed effects make
   comparisons within-relation, but they cannot make the sample representative.
3. **Gold exposure has little to bite on.** The subset is the top decile by
   co-occurrence, so the frequency confound is largely designed out — but so is much
   of the variation the exposure term would use, which is why `l_shared_static` is
   null (p=0.86) even though exposure protects strongly across the full dataset.
   `l_distract_static` does reach significance on the same subset, but only in
   strain's presence (p=0.034 with it, 0.18 without), so this is weak evidence that
   exposure signal survives the restriction — not a clean demonstration of it.
4. **Multiplicity.** Several feature families were tested against one panel, and the
   exposure control was itself respecified after seeing the results. The nominal
   p=0.0021 on subject strain is not adjusted for either. The reassurance is that
   strain held across all four exposure specifications tried (+0.153 to +0.189, p
   from 0.010 to 0.002) and the permutation p moved by 0.006.
5. **The LR tests are unclustered; the coefficient table is clustered.** Every chi2
   in the model-comparison table — the headline 18.3 included — comes from
   `fit()` without `cov_type="cluster"`, so it treats 3,932 rows as independent when
   they are ~6.3 rows per fact over 623 facts. Those chi2 values are therefore
   anti-conservative, and an LR test is not the right instrument under clustering
   anyway. The clustered Wald p is the conservative reading, and subject strain
   passes it comfortably (p=0.0021); `l_distract_static` does not always (LR p=0.048
   vs clustered Wald p=0.179 for the same term in row 4 above). **The permutation
   test is immune to this**, since the real and scrambled chi2 are computed the same
   way, so any anti-conservatism is shared and cancels — one more reason it is the
   test to trust here.
6. **`correct` is a substring match** — any alias longer than three characters
   anywhere in a 15-token greedy generation. Some of the 1,006 events are scoring
   flips rather than knowledge flips; an exact-match arm would bound this.
7. **Tokens are whitespace words.** BPE is implemented (`--bpe`) but not run; the
   frequency cutoff would need re-deriving for subword pieces.

---

## Reproducing

```bash
python feature_extraction/build_strain_panel.py \
    --recall-dir data/artifacts/expermints/15shot_trajectory_top10_internal_with_hidden/recall \
    --out data/artifacts/features/strain_panel_15shot_top10.parquet

```

Then regenerate every diagnostic quoted above — the model ladder, the exposure-spec
robustness table, the collinearity matrix, the ~46% sampling argument, the suppression
ladder, the strain-vs-distract contrast, the per-relation and windowed comparisons,
the inherited claims, and (with `--permutations`) the permutation test under all three
exposure specs:

```bash
python analysis/strain_diagnostics.py \
    --panel data/artifacts/features/strain_panel_15shot_top10.parquet \
    --out data/artifacts/features/strain_diagnostics_specE.txt \
    --permutations 150
```

Without `--permutations` it runs in seconds; with 150 it takes ~6 minutes (0.7s per
draw per spec). It writes a `.json` mirror beside the text log, so a future change can
be diffed numerically instead of by reading prose. There is no separate permutation
step: section 10 calls `null_control_distribution.run_permutations` and stores every
draw of the reported test in the JSON.

Optionally, render the figures. The report **fits nothing** — its only inputs are the
diagnostics JSON and the panel — so it can never disagree with the log above. The
null-distribution histogram in particular shows where the real chi2 sits inside the
permuted null far more directly than the summary line does. Add `--cdn` for a ~60 KB
page instead of ~4.8 MB.

```bash
python analysis/report_token_strain.py \
    --diagnostics data/artifacts/features/strain_diagnostics_specE.json \
    --panel data/artifacts/features/strain_panel_15shot_top10.parquet \
    --out analysis/report_token_strain_specE.html
```

Feature code `src/features/strain.py`; 15 regression tests in
`tests/test_strain_features.py`, covering the three mistakes this metric already
made — same-string/different-QID must count twice, an entity must not compete with
itself, and a subject must not be its own distractor.

**If you run `null_control_distribution.py` standalone, pass `--control-namelen`.**
(The diagnostics always tests against `BASE + NAMELEN`.) Without it the baseline is
exposure-only, and there the null distribution centres far from zero because
scrambled strain remains a proxy for name length — so both the real and the
scrambled feature beat that baseline for the same uninteresting reason, and the test
answers the wrong question.
